blocks.content: Imagine you and a friend decide to build a house. The architect draws up the big picture: three bedrooms, a garage, a garden facing east. That's the vision. But nobody picks up a hammer from that drawing alone.

Someone still has to decide exactly where every pipe runs, how thick each wall is, which socket goes on which switchboard. Low Level Design is that second, much more detailed set of decisions, applied to software instead of a house.
Low Level Design (LLD) is the process of translating a system's high level plan into the actual classes, objects, interfaces, and interactions that a developer can sit down and code directly.
1. What Low Level Design Actually Means
blocks.text: 1. What Low Level Design Actually Means

blocks.content: At its core, LLD answers one question, given that we already know what we are building, exactly how is each individual piece of it going to work internally.
1.1 The Blueprint Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845654941-601321874.png
blocks.alt: A vision becomes an architect blueprint, then an engineer detailed plan, then an actual building

blocks.content: An owner vision is vague on purpose, it needs to stay flexible. An architect blueprint, the high level design, commits to the overall shape, rooms, floors, load bearing walls. But a construction crew genuinely cannot build from that blueprint alone.
An engineer still has to specify exact pipe diameters, wire gauges, and joint types. That level of specification, precise enough to actually build from, is exactly what LLD is for software.
1.2 From "What" to "Exactly How"
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845656699-646478276.png
blocks.alt: HLD asks what to build, LLD asks exactly how each piece works

blocks.content: High Level Design decides what the system needs, a payment service, a notification service, a database. Low Level Design decides exactly how each of those pieces is actually built internally, which classes exist, what data they hold, how they talk to each other.

blocks.title: One level answers "what", the other answers "how"
blocks.content: This distinction is the cleanest way to keep HLD and LLD from blurring together in your head, and it is exactly what the next topic in this module explores in full depth.
2. Where LLD Sits in the Software Design Process
blocks.text: 2. Where LLD Sits in the Software Design Process

blocks.content: LLD does not happen in isolation, it is one specific stage in a larger pipeline that starts with a business need and ends with running code.
2.1 The Journey From Requirements to Code
blocks.text: 2.1 The Journey From Requirements to Code

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845658200-711207216.png
blocks.alt: Requirements flow into high level design, then low level design, then working code

blocks.content: Requirements describe the actual business problem in plain language. High Level Design breaks that problem into major components and how they connect. Low Level Design takes each of those components and works out its internal structure. Only then does actual code get written, and by this point, writing it is closer to typing than to deciding.

3. What LLD Actually Produces
LLD is not just a diagram exercise, it produces concrete, reusable artifacts that directly shape the code that gets written.
3.1 Classes, Interfaces, and Relationships
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845659563-544633698.png
blocks.alt: Classes, interfaces, and the relationships between them are the direct output of LLD

blocks.content: The most direct output of LLD is a set of classes, what data each one holds, what behavior it exposes, interfaces defining contracts between components, and the relationships connecting them all, association, composition, inheritance, each covered in its own topic later in this course.
3.2 Design Patterns as Reusable Solutions
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845661085-612698749.png
blocks.alt: A common recurring problem gets solved by a named, reusable pattern, applied to your actual classes

blocks.content: Many problems that show up during LLD are not actually new, someone has solved a very similar shaped problem before and given that solution a name, a design pattern. Recognizing that your situation matches a known pattern saves you from reinventing a solution from scratch.
4. A Concrete Example, Designing a Parking Lot Ticket System
blocks.text: 4. A Concrete Example, Designing a Parking Lot Ticket System

blocks.content: Abstract definitions only go so far, seeing LLD actually applied to a real, small problem makes the idea concrete.
4.1 The Vague Requirement
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845662515-826591583.png
blocks.alt: Build a parking system is genuinely ambiguous on its own and needs a concrete design first

blocks.content: "Build a parking system" sounds simple, but it genuinely does not tell you what a vehicle is, what a slot is, or how the two connect. That gap between a one line request and something you can actually code is precisely the gap LLD exists to close.
4.2 Turning It Into an LLD Sketch
blocks.text: 4.2 Turning It Into an LLD Sketch

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845663918-874895759.png
blocks.alt: ParkingLot, ParkingSlot, and Vehicle form a small class relationship for this example

blocks.content: A first LLD pass identifies the core entities, a ParkingLot that owns a collection of slots, a ParkingSlot that can be free or occupied, and a Vehicle that gets parked. Nothing here is complicated, but writing it down explicitly is what actually makes the system buildable.

Run this and it prints exactly two successful parkings and one rejection, since the lot only has two slots. Small, but this is genuinely a working piece of LLD, three classes, each with one clear responsibility, wired together correctly.
5. Why LLD Actually Matters
It would be reasonable to ask why any of this matters if the code eventually works either way, the honest answer is that it matters enormously once the system has to change.
5.1 Code That Survives Change
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845665587-145705719.png
blocks.alt: A new requirement means a small change for well designed code, but a widespread rewrite for poorly designed code

blocks.content: Real systems change constantly, a new vehicle type, a new pricing rule, a new slot category. A parking lot designed with clear classes and clean boundaries absorbs a change like this in one or two places. A system thrown together without that structure often needs changes scattered across the entire codebase for the exact same request.
5.2 What Happens Without It
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845667154-231219501.png
blocks.alt: Jumping straight to code produces tangled dependencies that are hard to extend later

blocks.content: Skipping LLD does not mean skipping design, it just means the design happens accidentally, buried inside whatever code gets typed first. That accidental design tends to tangle unrelated pieces together, making even a small future change surprisingly risky.
6. Common Misconceptions About LLD
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784845668664-838753913.png
blocks.alt: The myth that LLD is just UML diagrams versus the reality that LLD is the actual design decisions

blocks.content: A common misconception treats LLD as synonymous with drawing UML diagrams. The diagrams are a communication tool, the actual value is in the decisions behind them, which class owns which responsibility, which relationship genuinely fits, which pattern actually solves the problem at hand. You can do excellent LLD thinking with no diagram tool open at all.

blocks.title: The diagram is a record of the decision, not the decision itself
blocks.content: Two engineers can draw a nearly identical looking class diagram and still have designed genuinely different systems, because the real design work happened in the reasoning, not in the box and arrow drawing.
7. Key Takeaways

["Low Level Design translates a high level plan into the actual classes, interfaces, and interactions a developer can code directly","It sits between high level design and actual code in the overall software design pipeline, answering exactly how each component works internally","Its concrete outputs are classes, interfaces, relationships, and reusable design patterns, not just diagrams","Skipping deliberate LLD does not remove design from a system, it just makes that design accidental and much harder to change safely later"]
items: Low Level Design translates a high level plan into the actual classes, interfaces, and interactions a developer can code directly
It sits between high level design and actual code in the overall software design pipeline, answering exactly how each component works internally
Its concrete outputs are classes, interfaces, relationships, and reusable design patterns, not just diagrams
Skipping deliberate LLD does not remove design from a system, it just makes that design accidental and much harder to change safely later
